Although the treatise pairs each subsequent section of the sūtra text with the four general propositions individually, it first provides two expositions for the first three propositions and then offers two further expositions for the final proposition; as that treatise is extensive, it is difficult to comprehend upon a first reading, and one should follow this [present] interpretation.
Regarding this, the first explanation states:

"Furthermore, there is another meaning: 'various skillful means' refers to manifesting the various faults of the heterodox teachings of non-Buddhists and the various merits of the true Dharma of the Buddhas."

As it is said in the Sūtra: "Śāriputra, since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have extensively expounded the verbal teachings through innumerable skillful means to guide sentient beings, causing them to attain liberation from all points of attachment."
Although the phrasing differs slightly, the general meaning is the same.
There are four further sets of "innumerable skillful means" (upāya):

first, the skillful means of causing [beings] to enter into various wholesome dharmas; second, the skillful means of severing all doubts; third, the skillful means of causing [beings] to enter into superior and victorious wisdom; and fourth, the skillful means of gathering in sentient beings by relying on the four methods of attraction (saṃgrahavastu) so that they may attain liberation.

Among these six types of exegesis, turning away from the heterodox to enter the orthodox, advancing in the wholesome and destroying the unwholesome, entering supreme wisdom oneself, and causing others to attain liberation are assigned respectively.
By means of these skillful means, one attracts, gathers, leads, and guides all sentient beings so that they may be free from all attachments;
for "attachment" refers to grasping at the basis, as it is the root of craving and defilement within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
The treatise states:
"Those who are attached are attached to various things; they may be attached to realms (*dhātu*), attached to stages (*bhūmi*), attached to divisions (*pakṣa*), or attached to vehicles (*yāna*).
To be 'attached to realms' means to be attached to the three realms."

"Those who dwell on the ground" refers to those who dwell in the ground of precept-and-observance grasping (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), from the first dhyāna stage up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the stage of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*); taking these nine successive attainments as their ground, they are called "dwelling on the ground" because they cling to this samādhi through precept-and-observance grasping and view-grasping (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Attachment to the category of the householder consists of performing various karmas such as wrong views and the like, once one has become attached to the category of the householder;
attachment to the category of the renunciant consists of seeking fame and gain, which can give rise to various types of discursive thoughts and afflictions.

They are attached to the Śrāvaka vehicle because they delight in upholding minor precepts and seek the four fruits [of the śramaṇa]; they are attached to the Mahāyāna because they are attached to gain, offerings, and honor.
"This is because they observe various phenomena through the attachment to conceptualization, even up to the conceptualization of the stage of Buddhahood.
[The Sūtra says: "For what reason? ... until ... all are already fully perfected."
The commentary states:
This is the second phrase.
The first section of the treatise says:

"Furthermore, regarding 'various kinds of knowledge and vision,' because one's own body has accomplished inconceivable realms, it is distinct from those of the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas; as the sutra says: 'Śāriputra!'"
"Because the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, as well as his skillful means, have reached the other shore"; to have reached the other shore means to surpass all other bodhisattvas.
Although the phrasing differs slightly, the meaning is no different.

Regarding "knowledge and vision" (*jñāna-darśana*): these are the essences of the two wisdoms, the ultimate and the conventional. Fundamental wisdom is termed "knowledge," while subsequently attained wisdom is termed "vision.

Regarding "skillful means" (*upāya*): it refers to the wondrous application and skillful means of this wisdom. Because one personally accomplishes inconceivable realms, possessing both knowledge and vision—unlike the śrāvakas and others—is termed "skillful means."

“Pāramitā” means reaching the other shore. It clarifies that the Buddha has accomplished the essence of two supreme wisdoms; therefore, he is able to accomplish an inconceivable realm, having already reached the other shore and surpassed all others.

Because he possesses the wondrous function of the two wisdoms of skillful means, he can further cause others to reach the other shore; thus, by means of this inconceivable realm of knowledge and vision, he also bestows it upon the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.
Regarding the passage from "Śāriputra [attains] the Samādhi of Liberation," the commentary states:
This is the third phrase.
The first section of the treatise states:
"Furthermore, regarding 'various kinds of mindfulness and contemplation,' it is as the Sūtra says: 'Śāriputra!

Because the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are vast, profound, far-reaching, unobstructed, and unhindered, and because he is fully endowed with the powers, the fearlessnesses, the unique qualities, the faculties, the strengths, the factors of enlightenment, the meditative concentrations, the liberations, the samādhis, and the samāpattis.'"
The meaning of the text is largely the same, though there are slight differences in detail.

Here, "knowledge and vision" (jñāna-darśana) is described as "vast" because it is boundless; "great" because it is unsurpassed; "profound" because it is difficult to fathom; and "distant" because its duration extends through the long span of time until the end of the future.
The above constitutes the general summary of all these virtues.

They are termed "knowledge and vision" because their intrinsic nature consists of the two types of wisdom; furthermore, they are termed "knowledge and vision" because these virtues are also subsumed within the retinue of those two types of wisdom.
The passage beginning with "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) consists of distinct phrases concerning various virtues.
According to this scriptural text, "immeasurable" refers to the four immeasurables; thus, the treatise cites the scripture as being "unobstructed."
"Unimpeded" refers to the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*);
"powers" refers to the ten powers; and "fearlessnesses" refers to the four fearlessnesses.
The root treatise cites the uncommon qualities from the sūtra, which are the eighteen uncommon qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).

The "faculties" (indriya) refer to the five faculties; the "powers" (bala) refer to the five powers; and the "factors of enlightenment" (bodhipakṣa) refer to the thirty-seven. These four aforementioned categories are not present in the original versions of the sūtras.

"Dhyāna" refers to the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the form realm; "samādhi" refers to the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*); "vimokṣa" refers to the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*); "samāpatti" refers to the three concentrations (*trisamādhi*); and "samāpatti" [in this context] refers to the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvasamāpatti*). This particular version of the sūtra does not even contain these terms.

The treatise cites thirteen sections within the sutra; however, in this present sutra, there are eight sections combined whose merit is termed "mindful contemplation" (smṛtyupasthāna). Its essence is the wisdom of clear recollection and understanding, and thus it cannot be explained in detail.
Each category of meaning should be briefly analyzed; the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*) are analyzed by way of five headings:

first, listing the names; second, explaining the names; third, discerning their modes of activity (*ākāra*); fourth, identifying their essential nature (*svabhāva*); and fifth, discerning their distinctions.

Regarding the enumeration of the names, they are: immeasurable loving-kindness (*maitrī*), immeasurable compassion (*karuṇā*), immeasurable sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and immeasurable equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Regarding the explanation of the names: first, because these four arise by taking immeasurable objects as their focus, namely all sentient beings;
second, because they give rise to immeasurable practices, and both the practice and its understanding are likewise utterly vast.
Third, it is called "immeasurable" because it produces immeasurable fruits, attaining the merit of Great Brahmā and accomplishing the state of a Tathāgata;
fourth, this is a numerical term, explained as a numeral-based compound.
Regarding the analysis of its aspects: sentient beings within the dharma-realm are generally categorized into three types.
The first is those who experience neither suffering nor pleasure; bestowing happiness upon them without error is called *maitrī* (loving-kindness), which has non-hatred as its essence.
Second, regarding those who possess suffering, to extract their suffering is called compassion (*karuṇā*); its essence is non-harming.
Third, regarding those who possess happiness, to assist in their joy is called sympathetic joy (*muditā*); its essence is the absence of envy as a root of virtue.

Furthermore, one gives rise to the thought of detachment from ignorance regarding those who experience neither suffering nor pleasure; the thought of detachment from hatred regarding those who experience suffering; and the thought of detachment from greed regarding those who experience pleasure. Because one desires with equanimity that all beings be freed from these evils, it is called equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Because it causes one to abandon evil, its essence is wholesome abandonment.

To define its essential nature, three factors are combined: namely, non-hatred (*adveṣa*), non-harming (*ahiṃsā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). The essence of non-jealousy (*anīrṣyā*) is simply non-hatred, as there is no separate factor [other than that].
To distinguish their differences, each has three types:
first, the object-condition of sentient beings, wherein one forms the perception of a sentient being;
second, the object-condition of phenomena, wherein one does not perceive a sentient being but forms only the perception of a phenomenon.

The third is "without object" (*anālambana*): furthermore, because one is free from the mind of conceptual discrimination regarding all phenomena and forms the perception of *tathatā*, it is called "without object"; alternatively, it refers to the immeasurable phenomena that take all teachings as their objects.
Among these three, the first is shared with non-Buddhists, the second is shared with those of the two vehicles, and the last belongs exclusively to Bodhisattvas.
The first two bring about peace and happiness, while the last brings about benefit; the resulting fruits may thus be known.

Regarding the distinctions between [these four immeasurables] and Great Loving-kindness (maitrī), Great Compassion (karuṇā), Great Joy (muditā), and Great Equanimity (upekṣā): the former are exclusively real contemplations arising only from a Buddha, taking the three realms as their object, and are never associated with delusion (moha). These [immeasurables], however, pertain to both the conventional and the real, arise in both ordinary beings and noble ones, take indeterminate realms as their objects, and are not necessarily dissociated from delusion.
The four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are distinguished by way of three sections:
first, the enumeration of their names; second, the definition of their characteristics; and third, the determination of their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
As for the enumeration of their names:

There are four types of unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*): first, the unimpeded analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma*); second, the unimpeded analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha*); third, the unimpeded analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti*); and fourth, the unimpeded analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna*).

Regarding their characteristics: "phenomena" refers to the expressive names, phrases, and teachings; "meaning" refers to the principles of the ultimate and conventional truths that are expressed; "language" refers to the various regional dialects and sounds; and "eloquence" refers to the seven kinds of eloquence.
Because these four knowledges are free from all obstruction and hindrance, they are called the "unimpeded analytical knowledges" (pratisaṃvid).
They have many distinctions, as explained in the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, and the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra*.

Regarding their essential nature: these four have the untainted subsequently attained wisdom (*anāsrava-prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) as their essence, for they do not constitute the realization of suchness itself.

The unimpeded analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*) also extends to correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*); it is partially attained in the first stage (*bhūmi*), spontaneously perfected through the removal of obstructions in the ninth stage, and fully realized at the stage of Buddhahood.
The ten powers (*daśabala*) are briefly analyzed by way of five sections:

first, the definition of their names; second, the determination of their essence; third, their modes of activity (*ākāra*); fourth, their sequential order; and fifth, various supplementary categories.
Regarding the definition of their names, there are two parts:
First, the enumeration of names; second, the explanation of names.
Regarding the enumeration: first is the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*);

second is the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma (*karmasvakatā-jñānabala*), which in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (fascicle 53) is termed the power of knowledge regarding the maturation of karma (*karmavipāka-jñānabala*).

3. The power of knowledge regarding the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), liberations (vimokṣa), concentrations (samādhi), and attainments (samāpatti); this is called the power of knowledge regarding the defilement and purification of the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments;
4. The power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties (indriya) of beings;
5. The power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations (adhimukti).
Sixth, the power of knowledge regarding the various elements;
seventh, the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere, which is termed the power of knowledge regarding universal courses;
eighth, the power of knowledge regarding the recollection of past abodes.
Ninth is the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth;
tenth is the power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows.
To explain their names: the first is general, while the latter is specific.
The general meaning of "power" (*bala*) is the capacity to crush adversaries and the sense of being invincible.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Bodhisattvabhūmi, chapters 49 and 50; the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, chapter 57; the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, chapter 5; the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, chapter 4; the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, chapter 14; and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* all explain this characteristic as follows: it is called "power" because it possesses the functional capacity to bring about the benefit and happiness of sentient beings in every respect, and because its great majesty ultimately and completely overcomes all Māras and enemies. Thus, power is defined as that which, through its sovereign might, can crush what is otherwise difficult to subdue.
The *Abhidharma* states: "Because they skillfully subdue all māras and skillfully provide answers to questions and treatises, they are called the 'Ten Powers' (*daśabala*).
'Ten' refers to their number; because their functional applications differ, there are these ten kinds, and thus they are named the 'Ten Powers.'"
This is according to the "explanation by enumeration" (*saṃkhyā-vigraha*) among the six types of grammatical explanation.

To explain the specific names: when cause and effect correspond, it is called a "possible case" (*sthāna*); if they do not correspond, it is called an "impossible case" (*asthāna*). Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The causes that function in accordance with reality, such that pure and impure fruits are never discordant, are called 'possible cases'."

"Abode" (āyatana) has the meaning of establishment; it is called an "abode" because it serves as the basis for the arising of the object, and because it can establish the fruit by being able to give rise to the dharmas that constitute the fruit. Thus, the name "abode" is established on account of its causality.
The cause of inequality is the opposite of the aforementioned; this is called "impossible" (*asthāna*).
Regarding these two types, that which is omniscient, unimpeded, pure, and free from overweening pride is termed "knowledge" (*jñāna*); the meaning of its power (*bala*) is as previously described.

The three types of karma performed by each individual throughout the three periods of time—whether to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*), or as indeterminate (*aniyata*)—are called "one's own karma. Correctly knowing this is termed the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma (*karmasvakajñānabala*).
The arising of knowledge and understanding regarding the maturation of the results of wholesome and unwholesome karma is also called the power of knowing the maturation of karma.

Meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) refer to the four *dhyānas*; liberations (*vimokṣa*) refer to the eight liberations; meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) refer to all mental states of concentration; and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) refer to all mental and non-mental states of concentration. Correctly knowing these is called the power of knowing meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.

These various meditative concentrations (samādhi) are both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*); when designated as "defiled" (*saṃkliṣṭa*) or "pure" (*viśuddha*), they are termed "impure" and "pure.

The faculties (*indriya*) are the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*). Their states of being weak, medium, or superior are called "inferior" (*hīna*) and "superior" (*praṇīta*). The correct knowledge regarding these is the power of knowledge regarding the superiority and inferiority of the faculties (*indriyaparāparajñānabala*).
If one takes faith in another as the precursor, or takes the contemplation of all phenomena as the precursor, [the faculties] become weak, middling, or superior.
This joyful inclination and resolute conviction is called "diverse resolve"; the correct knowledge regarding this is termed the "power of knowing the diverse resolves" (*nānādhimukti-jñānabala*).

If one were to extensively establish various lineages—whether as one vehicle, three vehicles, four vehicles, or five vehicles; or as those whose temperaments are dominated by greed, hatred, or delusion, and so forth—even up to the eighty thousand types of conduct of sentient beings called "various realms" (*nānā-dhātu*), because a realm (*dhātu*) is a lineage (*gotra*), the correct knowledge regarding this is termed the "power of knowing the diverse elements" (*nānā-dhātu-jñāna-bala*).

If one practices in accordance with the various doors of rebirth (*gati*) in this very manner—such as practicing the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) for those whose temperament is characterized by craving—this is called "conduct leading everywhere" (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad*). It may refer to conduct leading to all five realms of existence; or to the various types of conduct associated with the diverse views of the various non-Buddhist *śramaṇas* and *brāhmaṇas*; or it refers to blameless conduct leading to this world or other worlds. Correctly knowing these is called the "power of knowledge regarding conduct leading everywhere," because one is able to fully understand the conduct that leads to all realms of existence; it is also termed "all-pervading conduct."

If, among the various assemblies of sentient beings, one establishes and designates the distinctions of categories through names and conventions in four directions—following the eight conventional expressions regarding all past individual existences:

first, such a name; second, the class of birth; third, the lineage; fourth, food and drink; fifth, the experience of suffering and pleasure; sixth, longevity; seventh, duration of stay; and eighth, the limit of the lifespan.
Among these eight, one briefly recollects six types of past conduct; there are immeasurable varieties of recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*).

The six brief modes of conduct are: first, the conventional designation of names; second, distinctions of caste and class such as *kṣatriya* and so forth; third, parents; fourth, the manner of food and drink; fifth, prosperity and decline; and sixth, the span of life.

These past abodes are objects of the past; because they reside in the past world, the knowledge that arises with respect to these past abodes, accompanied by mindfulness and recollection, is called the power of the knowledge of recollecting past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānabala*).

When sentient beings are about to pass away, it is called the time of death; when they abide in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it is called the time of birth. The power of knowledge regarding death and birth (*cyutyupapādajñānabala*) is the ability to correctly know both the time of death and the time of birth within the good and evil realms of existence.

The permanent and complete eradication of all outflows (*āsrava*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) in all phenomena without exception is called the "exhaustion of outflows" (*āsravakṣaya*). Correct knowledge regarding this is termed the "power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows" (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*).
Here, "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is the essence and "power" (*bala*) is its function; however, knowledge itself is the power, as there is no distinct nature between them.
Among these, the power of knowledge consisting of the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñānabala*) is the proximate explanation.

All others, from the first [power] regarding the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna*) up to the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), are the objects of observation, while the power of knowledge is the observing wisdom.

The powers of knowledge (jñānabala) ranging from the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (sthānāsthāna-jñāna) up to the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-jñāna) are all analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.

"Past lives" (*pūrvanivāsa*) is the object, and the power of knowledge associated with recollection (*anusmṛti-samprayukta-jñānabala*) is the perceiver; this is also analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* compound.

Second, regarding the essential nature [of the faculties]: the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, fascicle 57, states, “The Buddha possesses the faculty of complete knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*), which has the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) as its essence. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states, “Whether it be meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or wisdom (*prajñā*), along with their associated mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states, “That is to say, the five faculties collectively constitute its intrinsic nature.”
Although these three texts differ, their essence consists of five types:
first, the most excellent essence; thus, according to the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, the Buddha’s faculty of knowing all and the faculty of wisdom constitute its nature.
Second, regarding the nature of that which is produced: the *Abhidharmakośa* states that it consists of either concentration (*samādhi*) or wisdom (*prajñā*).

Third, regarding the actual nature [of the powers]: the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that their essence is the five faculties (*pañcendriya*). Because wisdom is predominant, the ten powers are said to have wisdom as their intrinsic nature; thus, they are referred to only as the "power of knowledge regarding the possible and the impossible" (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), and not as the power of faith, the power of diligence, and so forth. Based on this, the passage from the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* is fully explained.

Fourth, the essence of association (*saṃprayukta*): the *Abhidharma* further states that "it has as its nature the four aggregates of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that are associated with it.

Fifth, the essence of the retinue (*parivāra*): it has the five aggregates as its nature, because it takes as its essence the unconditioned form (*rūpa*) and so forth that assist it, such as the form associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-samvara*) and the form associated with the Path (*mārga-samvara*).

Although there is no explicit textual authority for this, it must necessarily be so according to principle, because it prevents the defilement of violating the precepts and assists in crushing the enemy.
The remaining three gates are as explained in the second fascicle of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā*.
The four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) are analyzed by way of five gates:

first, the definition of their names; second, the determination of their essence (*svabhāva*); third, their modes of activity (*ākāra*); fourth, their sequential order; and fifth, various supplementary gates. These are as presented in the fifth chapter of the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, the fifty-third [chapter] of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the fourth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, the fiftieth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, and the fourteenth chapter of the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā*.
The analysis of the names has two parts:
first, the enumeration of the names; second, the explanation of the names.

Regarding the enumeration of the names: first, the fearlessness of perfect enlightenment; second, the fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows; third, the fearlessness regarding obstructive dharmas; fourth, the fearlessness regarding the path leading out of suffering.
There are two ways of explaining the name: first, the general, and second, the specific.
Regarding the general: "four" is a numerical designation;

"fearlessness" refers to being able to know these four matters for oneself with such composure that one is without fear, the mind is free from timidity or inferiority, there is no doubt or suspicion, and one is entirely devoid of alarm—therefore, it is called "fearlessness."
Regarding the alternative names: because he has perfectly awakened to all phenomena and equally awakened to all phenomena, he is called the "Perfectly Awakened One" (Samyaksaṃbuddha).
Because he has severed all afflictions, outflows, seeds, and manifestations, he is called the "One Whose Outflows are Exhausted" (Kṣīṇāsrava).
Regarding the teaching on obstructive phenomena (*āvaraṇa-dharma*): since defilement necessarily constitutes an obstruction, they are called "obstructive phenomena.
Regarding the teaching on the path to liberation: because the noble ones, through cultivation, definitely emerge from suffering, it is called "the path to emerging from suffering."
Regarding these four, the attainment of fearlessness is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
As for its essential nature, the fifty-seventh [chapter] states that it has faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, and the faculty of having already known as its nature.

The *Abhidharma* states: "Whether it be concentration or wisdom, along with the various mental states and mental factors associated with them"; it further says: "If it functions as the nature of subsequently attained knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), or if it abides in its own nature as the essence of correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)."

This essence has five aspects: in terms of its excellence, it takes the two types of wisdom as its essence; in terms of its initiation, it takes concentration and discernment as its essence; in terms of its reality, it takes the five faculties as its essence; in terms of its association, it takes the four aggregates as its nature; and in terms of its retinue, it takes the five aggregates as its essence.

Regarding the mode of activity (*ākāra*): as the Sūtra says, "The Blessed One himself declares, 'I am a Perfectly Awakened One. Furthermore, when a śramaṇa or a non-śramaṇa comes from another region, the Buddha greets him, saying, 'Are you dwelling in peace and well-being?'"
"Can one obtain alms?
Thereupon, someone raised this objection:
"If it is said that the Perfectly Awakened One has nothing he does not know, how is it that he now asks another person? This is quite contradictory."
Regarding this challenge, I see no grounds for it;
I abide in security, free from fear and dread, and declare myself to occupy the exalted position of a Great Sage. Why is this so?

He receives those who come so as to cause them to give rise to the supreme resolve; for by hearing the Buddha’s words of consolation, they develop the mind set on the Way. He wishes to lead all people to examine matters with precision: if even the Buddha, who already knows, still asks, how much more so others who do not know?

Furthermore, he establishes a model for future generations; seeing those who have resolved to attain enlightenment, he should guide and gather them in. It is not that the Buddha is unaware, yet he still speaks of being "Equal Enlightenment" (Samyaksambodhi).
Moreover, as a sutra says: "I have exhausted all outflows" (āsravakṣaya).
Later, when Devadatta committed various evil deeds, the Buddha constantly rebuked him;
yet when Upāli was disciplined and compliant, the Buddha always spoke to him with gentle words.
Consequently, someone raised this objection:

To say that all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted and all afflictions (*kleśa*) have vanished, while simultaneously rebuking Devadatta and speaking with affectionate words to Sunakṣatra—how can the outflows possibly be exhausted as long as greed and hatred have not been extinguished?
How utterly contradictory this is!
Regarding this objection, I see no grounds for it;

I abide in security, free from fear and dread, and declare myself to occupy the exalted position of a Great Sage. Devadatta is like a wicked horse that requires harsh punishment to be tamed, and if one does not rebuke him, he instead says, "I am afraid of you.

Wisdom is likened to a sun-like elephant that follows the human mind; therefore, it can be tamed through gentle words. This is not because I possess greed or hatred, nor that my outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet exhausted.

Furthermore, as the Sūtra states, the Buddha taught his disciples that obstructive factors (*āvaraṇadharma*) are necessarily obstacles to defilement; yet he did not prohibit those who have attained the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) or Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) from having wives and children.
Thereupon, a challenge was raised:
"If defilement necessarily constitutes an obstacle, how is it that the Sages kept wives and children? This is truly contradictory.
Regarding this challenge, I find no way to provide a correct explanation.

The state of the Great Sage (Maharṣi) is a place of peace and freedom from fear; yet, improper conduct obstructs the various noble paths, and maintaining a wife obstructs the path of detachment from desire. Since those who have attained the first two fruits of the path have not yet abandoned desire, and because their natural precepts (prakṛti-śīla) have long been established, they exclude improper conduct; however, what fault is there in not severing ties with one's wife and children?
Therefore, all defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) are not without obstruction.

Furthermore, as a sutra states: "I have taught the path of transcendence for my disciples; through the cultivation of this by the noble ones, there is certain transcendence and certain penetration. Yet, there was the Arhat Kālodāyin, who was beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), whose feet were buried in excrement, and Aṅgulimāla, whose body was consumed by the fires of hell.
Thereupon, a difficult objection was raised:

"The Noble Path is cultivated for a long time with the hope of escaping all suffering; yet if those who have attained the stage of No-more-learning (aśaikṣa) must still undergo suffering upon returning, what is the use of practicing the Path?
How utterly contradictory this is!"
Regarding this objection, I see no valid basis for it:

the state of a Great Sage (maharṣi), which is secure and free from fear, truly constitutes the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa-phala); once attained, suffering is certainly eliminated. Since present causes must inevitably result in future retribution, it is for this reason that the Noble One undergoes suffering in the present in order to give rise to subsequent instruction.

Alternatively, the maturation of suffering is not experienced by one in the stage of no-more-learning because their evil karma has been exhausted; were there such [unexhausted] karma, it would necessarily obstruct the fruit and prevent the attainment of no-more-learning.

Regarding the statement that those who experience such suffering are "those beyond training" (aśaikṣa): although they currently abide as those still in training (śaikṣa) and have not yet abandoned desire, they are designated by that name because they are certain to become those beyond training. Even if they have attained supernatural powers (abhijñā), they are not [yet] Non-returners (anāgāmin) and the like, because their fivefold supernormal powers are merely worldly ones.

Alternatively, the suffering of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is not summoned by karma, because all karmic fruition (vipāka) must have already been exhausted. As explained in the twenty-ninth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* regarding the three periods of karma, it states that upon reaching the stage of no-more-learning, all evil karma is eliminated and will never again be experienced. It further explains that what is called "fixed karma" (niyata-karma) refers to those who have not yet entered the noble state (ārya), whereas for those who have entered the noble state, it is no longer termed fixed karma. As extensively detailed therein, an Arhat certainly possesses no fruit of suffering.
The latter two gates are also as explained in the commentary on the second fascicle of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*.

"Dhyāna" refers to the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*): namely, the first absorption with applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*); the second, free from applied and sustained thought but possessing joy (*prīti*); the third, free from joy and possessing bliss (*sukha*); and the fourth, free from both joy and bliss, characterized by equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and purity.

The concentrations consist of the four formless states, namely: the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
As for the liberations, they refer to the eight liberations, which are analyzed by way of three gates:
first, listing their names; second, clarifying their modes of activity; and third, establishing their essential natures.

Regarding the enumeration of these names, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (sections 12, 15, and 73), the fourth chapter of the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*, as well as the *Abhidharma-samuccaya* (section 13), the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (sections 4, 2, and 20), and the fourth chapter of the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, they are stated as follows:

1. The liberation of one possessing internal form who perceives external forms; 2. The liberation of one who is internally without perception of form and perceives external forms; 3. The liberation of the pure form, which is realized through bodily witness and fully attained; 4. The liberation of the sphere of infinite space; 5. The liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness; 6. The liberation of the sphere of nothingness; 7. The liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; 8. The liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling, which is realized through bodily witness and fully attained.

Regarding the manifestation of the modes of activity, the *Abhidharmakośa* (Chapter 29) states: "Internal perception of form while observing external forms is called the first liberation; not yet having internally subdued or eliminated the perception of form, one observes external forms as impure—this is called 'observing external forms.'"

Now, this is not the case; according to the text of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, for a beginner who, while still in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), has already abandoned the desires of the desire realm but has not yet suppressed or eliminated the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) by relying on the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) because they have not yet abandoned the desires of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

If one has long practiced the training and is already free from desire for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the visualizer establishes and brings before him the perception of forms; he then contemplates all internal and external forms within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as being of the nature of light. Because he has induced the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) by means of the three preceding liberations (*vimokṣa*), he contemplates the few or many forms subsumed under the spheres of mastery as being of the nature of light. He conceives of them as light because he has removed the obstacle to transformation (*nirmāṇāvaraṇa*); however, because he has not removed the obstacle of sensual craving, he does not conceive of them as impure.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states only that one who has not yet attained the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*) and has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), while contemplating external forms, possesses the first liberation; this is because it speaks solely in reference to the beginner practitioner.

Regarding the second liberation, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: having internally suppressed and eliminated the perception of form as a viewer, one contemplates only external objects as impure; this is called "having no internal perception of form while contemplating external forms."

In the Mahāyāna it is not so; according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, it says: "For those who have practiced for a long time, having already relied upon the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) to suppress and eliminate the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), the perception of the absence of form (*arūpa-saṃjñā*) is established and present before them as beginners. They then contemplate external forms, forming perceptions of them as small, large, and so forth. This differs from the initial stage where one contemplates both internal and external forms as being entirely luminous, because [the practitioner] has not yet attained mastery."

Now, this refers to observing external forms—such as those that are small or large—which have already been separated from desire for the realm of form; they are designated as "external" because they are free from defilement, and the observation is somewhat abbreviated because the mind's mastery has gradually increased.

Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Furthermore, one does not contemplate those signs of clarity through conceptualization, but instead forms a resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding external forms. One contemplates them as small, large, and so forth, rather than as light and so on. Since that which has already attained freedom from desire is designated as 'external,' one contemplates only those forms free from defiled color, which are thus termed 'external.'"

Furthermore, because the first liberation contemplates form without mentioning "external," and its internal possession of form likewise does not mention "internal," it universally takes as its object the forms of both internal and external faculties and objects, forming the perception of light. Therefore, in this second [liberation], regarding the internal possession of form, since there are forms such as the faculties, one contemplates external forms by observing only the external objects as being small, large, and so forth; one does not take the faculties and so on as objects to be observed as small, large, and so forth.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* further states: "Regarding the statement that 'the formless meditative absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*) do not manifest,' this refers to the observation of external forms without relying on the formless absorptions, because the formless absorptions cannot take external forms as their object. Alternatively, for one who has already abandoned desire for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), even without relying on the formless absorptions to suppress and eliminate the perception of form, they may rely solely on the form meditative absorptions; in such a case, the perception of formlessness manifests for the observer, and thus this statement was made."

Regarding the two aforementioned liberations (*vimokṣa*), one first forms the perception of light and subsequently forms the perceptions of the "small" and the "great"; thus, there is a distinction between these two contemplations, being broad at the beginning and narrow at the end.
The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (Chapter 20) states that these two liberations eliminate the obstacles to transformation (*nirmāṇa-āvaraṇa*) so that one may attain mastery over transformations.

Since the transformation [of mind] is pervasive because it exists within the four dhyānas, the first two liberations (vimokṣa) are based upon all four dhyānas; however, the first primarily relies on them. While the first two dhyānas exist only in their fundamental stages and not in the preparatory stages (sāmantaka), those [preparatory stages] lack the fruit of supernormal powers (abhijñā-phala) because they are characterized by a state of eager striving. This [liberation], however, involves a relaxed cultivation and thus possesses the fruit of supernormal powers. Consequently, it differs from the *Abhidharmakośa*, which holds that the first two dhyānas can eliminate the craving for visible forms (rūpa-rāga) in the desire realm, and that one therefore practices the meditation on the foul (aśubha-bhāvanā) within the first dhyāna.

Regarding the third liberation, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that it is established because the aspect of purity transforms into a pure, luminous, and fresh radiance, as its mode of activity (ākāra) shifts; furthermore, this occurs only in the fourth dhyāna because the mind is free from the eight afflictions and is thus exceptionally clear and pure. Although similar liberations exist in other stages, they are not established [as formal liberations] because they lack such preeminence (*ādhipatya*).

Now, regarding the Mahāyāna: suppose there is one who has already attained the perfection of equanimity and mindfulness that is pure and bright, and relying upon this, cultivates the complete purity of noble conduct. Within internal forms—both pure and impure—they have attained the perception of mutual dependence, the perception of mutual inclusion, and the perception of mutual single-flavor. This is the third liberation (*vimokṣa*). That is to say, by depending on various pure forms, they regard other forms as impure; it is not that they do not depend [on the former]. Because they see only a single category and lack the two cognitions of "pure" and "impure," this is called the first perception.

Furthermore, the nature of impurity enters into what is pure, and the nature of purity enters into what is impure; because that which is commonly called "pure" is covered by a thin skin that acts as an obstruction, thirty-six kinds of impure things are manifest within it—this is the second perception.
Proceeding in this manner, one synthesizes all forms into a single taste of pure perception; this is the third perception, which is called "accomplished.

It occurs only in the stage of the fourth dhyāna because of the purity of equanimity and mindfulness, because the treatises state that it transcends both suffering and pleasure, because all agitation has been stilled, and because it is well-polished; other stages are not so, therefore it is only in the fourth. This, too, involves observing external forms while internally having no perception of form.
Since these have already been discussed previously, they will not be elaborated upon here; rather, their distinct designations are established.

Regarding the next four formless liberations (*ārūpya-vimokṣa*), the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that they have the wholesome states of the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) as their nature. They are neither neutral nor defiled, because they are already liberated; nor do they have the nature of mundane wholesome states, because those are weak and inferior.

The path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) of the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) also receives the name "liberation," yet this is not the case for the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), because its object of focus (*ālambana*) is inferior. That [path] must turn its back upon the lower stage to be called "liberation"; therefore, the fundamental dhyānas (*maula-dhyāna*) are primarily discussed, as the preparatory stages are not complete in that regard.

Now, those of the Mahāyāna have already abandoned desire for their own level; relying on their own fundamental stage, they repeatedly contemplate the objects of that same level, engaging in reflection and resolute conviction to cause obstacles to recede further and to induce the arising of superior virtues.

That is to say, there is one who has already attained freedom from desire regarding the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*); they then contemplate and resolve upon that very sphere of space—this is called the mode of activity for the liberation of the sphere of infinite space.

Having already attained freedom from desire regarding the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), they then contemplate and resolve upon that very consciousness—this is called the mode of activity for the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness.

Having already attained freedom from desire regarding the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), they then contemplate and resolve upon the sphere of infinite consciousness—this is called the mode of activity for the liberation of the sphere of nothingness.

The two names, "emptiness" (*ākāśa*) and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), are designated according to the objects and modes of activity (*ākāra*) of their respective stages. The stage of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is named for the absence of consciousness; therefore, one forms a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the sphere of consciousness. Having already attained detachment from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one no longer forms a resolute conviction toward anything else. Rather, one forms a resolute conviction toward whatever place a perception (*saṃjñā*) can arise; the stage of Nothingness is called such because it is a place where perception can arise. Now, taking these minds and mental factors of "nothingness" as its object, it is called the sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Thus, one forms a resolute conviction toward this throughout its entirety, as will be understood below.
The preceding explanation regarding the departure from defilement was spoken with reference to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"The first seven liberations are attained by one who has already attained liberation and gives rise to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), and by one who has realized them through the body (*kāyasākṣin*)."

Regarding this, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, there are two masters' explanations: one says that by subduing the defilements of the first dhyāna and above, one attains the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*); the other says that by subduing the defilements of the fourth dhyāna and above, one attains the attainment of cessation.
Below the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), there exists the sense of subduing defilements, which causes obstacles to recede further and draws forth superior qualities;
however, within the single stage of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), one is certainly unable to subdue them.

Therefore, in the twelfth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, regarding the two liberations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), some say that the phrase "separation from the defilements of one's own stage" (*svabhūmi-kleśa-virāga*) is mentioned.

However, for the two higher stages, there is no mention of the words "separation from the defilements of one's own stage. This is because [the text] employs an abbreviated expression by implication (*saṃkṣepokti*) regarding both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); furthermore, these [liberations] exist only in the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*) and not in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).

The liberation of cessation (*nirodha-vimokṣa*) is taught as being both small and great; it is the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) itself, yet it lacks active mental formations because perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) have been abandoned.

Nevertheless, at the time of entering it, there are two modes of mental formation: namely, the ideation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and the ideation of the signless realm (*animitta-dhātu*). This is because these two—the initial cultivation and the long-term maturation—are clearly manifest upon entry.

Regarding their essential natures, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that the first three have non-attachment as their nature, while their attendants have the five aggregates as their nature; the next four immaterial absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) have wholesome states as their nature; and the eighth has cessation (*nirodha*) as its nature.

Within the seventy-three fascicles of the *Mahāyāna*, the explanation of the five dharmas states that their essence consists of mundane and supramundane right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). That which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) takes mundane right knowledge within the realm of conceptualization as its essence; that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) consists of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Having wisdom alone as its nature, it takes as its objects form, the formless, and the realm of suchness (*tathatā*). It is free from all obstacles to meditative concentration and induces superior virtues, for no other [faculty] possesses this capacity.

If they are of the nature of association (*saṃprayukta*), the first seven [liberations] have the four aggregates as their intrinsic nature, while their retinue has the five aggregates as its nature; thus the *Abhidharma* states:

"Whether it be concentration or wisdom, along with the various minds and mental factors associated with them—in the formless realm, because one reckons that there is the non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) of the meditative path—the eighth liberation has as its nature the functional capacity of the mind to become weary through twenty-two types of dharmas, which are subsumed under the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*)."

"Samādhi" is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "equipoise" (samāhita). This refers to the three types of equipoise—namely, emptiness (śūnyatā), signlessness (animitta), and wishlessness (apraṇihita)—which will be explained in detail below.
In the fifty-third fascicle of the *Prajñā[pāramitā]*, it states: "The three objects are identical because they both take emptiness as their object.

In the commentary’s re-explanation of the aforementioned three phrases, the second round of explanation for the subsequent three phrases states:

"Furthermore, the first [point] establishes that because those sentient beings who are capable of being transformed rely upon a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), it means that one is able to guide those transformable beings who possess the nature of enlightenment (*bodhigotra*) but have not yet resolved their minds toward awakening, causing them to rely on virtuous friends and abandon all attachments; this is called 'skillful means for guiding sentient beings.'"

The second is the perfection of skillful means and insight (*upāya-jñāna-darśana-pāramitā*), which brings about liberation for sentient beings whose faculties have matured; that is to say, it causes those who have long cultivated the aspiration for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) to attain liberation.

The third accomplishment consists of the purification through the subjugation of power, lineage, and mastery. This is called the Tathāgata’s vast and profound knowledge and vision.

This second phrase refers to the "accomplishment of speech" (*vāg-vibhūti*).
It is so called because the Buddha attains five kinds of exquisite vocal qualities when preaching all dharmas.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that five kinds of vocal sounds issue from the Buddha’s mouth:

first, they are as profound as thunder; second, they are clear and penetrating, heard from afar, and bring joy to those who hear them; third, they enter the heart and inspire reverence and love; fourth, they are precise and easy to understand; and fifth, listeners never tire of hearing them, for they can distinguish meanings such as those pertaining to the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*).

That which is profound like thunder is called the "differentiation of various dharmas"; that which is clearly understood and easy to comprehend is called the "skillful exposition of dharmas"—the term "dharmas" here applies generally to the aforementioned differentiation. That which, out of compassion and pity for the listeners, never tires them, and whose words are gentle, clear, and heard from afar, bringing joy to those who hear and entering their hearts with reverence and love, is called "delighting the minds of the multitude."
The first three [categories] each comprise one, while the last one subsumes two.

In the second section of the treatise, the various types of verbal expressions are again explained by means of seven phrases, which are correlated with these seven phrases as follows:
first, because various Dharma-gates gather in sentient beings and cause them to enter the Buddha-dharma, they penetrate deeply into the boundless.

Second, because it causes one to dwell without distraction, it guides sentient beings through instruction, causing them to dwell single-mindedly upon their objects without distraction due to their aspiration to hear [the Dharma]; thus, they are able to differentiate various phenomena in manifold ways.

Fifth, it causes that practitioner to achieve the attainment of the remedial dharma; by causing the practitioner to attain the remedial dharma of the nature of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), they are able to exhaustively fathom the true mark of all phenomena.

Seventh, it causes them to attain non-retrogression in their practice; and for those who have brought their practice to fulfillment, it ensures that they do not lose the benefit of teaching it to others.
The Buddha is able to expound the essentials of all dharmas because he has himself realized these seven aspects; thus, he can cause sentient beings to gradually follow his deeds.

The sequence can be understood, but fearing prolixity, it is not further detailed; therefore, the treatise says:
"Furthermore, 'accomplishing through teaching and transformation' refers to relying on the realization of the Dharma;
furthermore, 'accomplishment' refers to relying on the preaching of the Dharma.
These two kinds of Dharma are as previously explained.
The treatise states:
"Regarding these two kinds of dharmas, what is their sequence?
Based upon them, practitioners ask about realization and explain the sequence according to which they practice."

Regarding the instruction that "the preceding phrases should be understood as being repeated," it should be known that the preceding treatise repeats three types—expedient means (*upāya*), knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*), and mindfulness and observation (*smṛtyupasthāna*)—and subsequently provides a further explanation of the sequence of the seven phrases according to the order of realization; thus, the sequence is established according to the order of exposition.
Since the explanation is thus, practicing and studying in accordance with it leads to the realization of the successive stages; this concludes the preceding meaning.
It is intended to inform students that, within this first section of the analysis of the four propositions, the second concerns the accomplishment of teaching and transformation.
The fourth [section] explains the accomplishment of two kinds of distinctions.

Since the Dharma taught by the Buddha is taught based on realization, the treatise cites a sūtra containing five points: namely, what kind of dharma, how [is] the dharma, what it resembles, what its characteristics are, and what its essence is.
The treatise provides four interpretations.

The first set relies on the interpretation of abandoning the provisional and returning to the ultimate vehicle (*yāna*). First, it explains the names of the three vehicles as "what kind of dharmas" they are;
next, regarding each individual vehicle, it explains the various phenomena arising therein as "how such dharmas are."
Next, based on the gate of the three vehicles, one practices purity; this is called the "Dharma of What It Resembles.
Next, it is clarified that the three vehicles are but a single characteristic; this is called the "Dharma of What Its Characteristic Is.
Finally, there is ultimately only the One Buddha Vehicle with no essence of two vehicles; this is called the "Dharma of What Its Essence Is."
The second [method] is based on successive etymological explanations of phenomena (*dharma*).

What are phenomena? They are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena. How are they defined? They are defined as those arising from causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and those not arising from causes and conditions. That which arises from causes and conditions explains the conditioned; that which does not arise from causes and conditions explains the unconditioned.

What is the nature of phenomena? It refers to such categories as the permanent and the impermanent. The permanent is explained as not being produced by causes and conditions, while the impermanent is explained as being produced by causes and conditions.

What are the characteristics of phenomena? They refer to the three characteristics of arising and so forth, and the three characteristics of non-arising and so forth. By means of phenomena such as arising, the former [the impermanent] is explained; by means of non-arising and so forth, the permanent is explained.

What constitutes the substance of phenomena refers to those phenomena whose substance consists of the five aggregates and those whose substance does not consist of the five aggregates; that is, the five aggregates themselves, which are birth and so forth, and that which is neither the aggregates nor birth and so forth.

The third section explains only the latter three phrases, interpreting them solely in terms of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); as for the first two phrases, they do not differ from what was previously explained, and therefore they are not further analyzed here.
The treatise states:
"What is the nature of phenomena? It refers to phenomena that are impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated.
What are the characteristics of phenomena? It refers to phenomena such as the characteristic of being visible."

Regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmas*), it refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as both the grasper and the grasped; for the five aggregates are the basis of the accumulation of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya*), and they are also the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).
This may be understood according to the treatise.

The fourth [category] is explained according to the function of the Dharma in its teaching. As for "what the Dharma is," it refers to the fact that it is taught by means of the bodies of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and syllables (*vyañjana-kāya*).
As for "how the Dharma is," it refers to the fact that it is taught based upon the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata.

As for "what the Dharma resembles," it refers to its ability to teach and transform sentient beings who are capable of being taught. As for "what the characteristics of the Dharma are," it refers to its apprehension by means of sound; that is to say, it causes the listener to apprehend the signified Dharma by relying upon the sound.

Regarding "the nature of phenomena as conventional designations": because the characteristics of phenomena are conventionally designated as having an essential nature, although one is led to apprehend the expressed phenomena based on sounds, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) transcends verbal expression.

Thus, that which is expressed is a conventional designation of an essential nature and does not correspond to the reality of phenomena; this is so that one does not give rise to attachment by relying merely on the words.
However, fearing that people might not understand the current scriptural text, the translators followed the second method of successive interpretation (*krama-vyākhyāna*) to explain it.
Yet, as this was slightly out of sequence, they rectified it according to the meaning so as not to contradict the holy teachings;
had they explained it according to a different sense, it would have been merely a matter of human sentiment rather than the holy teachings.

Such characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and such nature (*svabhāva*) constitute the first category of phenomena; this is because characteristics are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) while nature is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Such essence (*ātman*) constitutes the fifth category of phenomena, namely, the essence of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and the non-essence of the five aggregates; these are combined to form the text.
Such power and such agent together constitute the third "what-like" dharma: power refers to permanent dharmas, because permanent dharmas possess the capacity for power;
the agent refers to impermanent dharmas, because they possess the quality of volitional activity.

Such causes, such conditions, such fruits, and such retributions—this constitutes the second category of "dharmas. Within these causes, conditions, fruits, and retributions, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are dharmas produced by causes and conditions, whereas unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are not dharmas produced by causes and conditions.
The meaning of establishing [a result] is called "cause" (*hetu*); the meaning of accomplishing a retribution is called "condition" (*pratyaya*).
That which directly obtains the result is called "cause"; that which indirectly obtains the result is called "condition.
The four fruits are called "fruits" (*phala*); the ripening [result] is called "retribution" (*vipāka*).

Thus, this beginning and end constitutes the fourth characteristic of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). The three characteristics of arising and so forth are the "end," because their essence is that of a phenomenon (*vastu*);
the three characteristics of non-arising and so forth are the "beginning," because their essence is that of principle (*tattva*).
Regarding "ultimate equality" (*atyanta-samatā*): this is a re-explanation of the fundamental principle, namely that the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is ultimate.

In the root treatise, following the sutra, it asks: "What more is there? How is it? What is it like? What are its characteristics? What is its essence? The Buddha again uses these [questions] to reveal that the five preceding meanings have no further distinct principles.
